Fig. 1 | The complex role of AMPs during infection in animal and plant  
hosts and environments. a, Representative host defence peptide (HDP) 
functions in animals, including recruitment of immune cells (for example, 
macrophages and lymphocytes), chemoattracting neutrophils (represented  
by the arrow), regulation of inflammation, direct microbial killing and 
modulation of cytokine production110. Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation 
by bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or host-derived damage-associated 
molecular patterns (DAMPs) leads to mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)  
and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signalling, driving immune responses. This 
process can be inhibited by HDPs such as LL-37, which bind to LPS and prevent 
recognition by TLR4, thereby downregulating MAPK and NF-κB signalling and 
modulating the inflammatory response110,111. b, Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) 
are degraded in the environment in farming and livestock contexts, which 
minimizes the impact on the natural environmental microbiota and reduces  
selective pressure for resistance development in these microbial communities 
in contrast with conventional antibiotics5. c, In plants, AMPs have a key role 
in innate immunity, responding to microbial infection by interacting with 
membrane lipids or kinase receptors. The plant cell surface is depicted with  
two pattern recognition receptor (PRR) complexes: one composed of flagellin 
sensing 2 (FLS2), BRI1-associated receptor kinase 1 (BAK1) and the bacterial 
flagellin-derived peptide flg22 (FLS2–BAK1–flg22), which signals via a leucine-
rich repeat (LRR) domain; and another formed by chitin elicitor receptor kinase 1  
(CERK1), LysM-containing receptor-like kinase 5 (LYK5) and the fungal cell

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 2 | Structures, mechanisms of action and distinctive targets of AMPs. 
a, Representatives of the structural diversity of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). 
The different classes are exemplified by linear extended indolicidin (Protein Data 
Bank (PDB): 1G89), α-helical magainin II (PDB: 2MAG), β-structured gomesin 
(PDB: 1KFP), mixed α-structured and β-structured human defensin (PDB: 1FD4) 
and the cyclic peptide cyclotide (PDB: 7RMR). b, The membranolytic mechanism 
of action of AMPs illustrated by several models. In the toroidal pore model 
represented by magainin II (PDB: 2MAG), peptides induce curvature of the lipid 
bilayer, forming pores lined by both peptide molecules and lipid headgroups; 
this can also occur in a less structured form, referred to as the disordered toroidal 
pore model. For the aggregate model followed by translocation by polyphemusin I 
(PM1) (PDB: 1X7K), peptides cluster on the membrane surface and translocate 
across the bilayer as peptide–lipid complexes, forming transient, irregular 
pores. Finally, for the carpet-like model represented by aurein 1.2 (PDB: 1VM5), 
peptides accumulate on the membrane surface and, upon reaching a threshold 
concentration, disrupt the bilayer in a detergent-like manner. In the barrel-stave 
model represented by dermcidin (PDB: 2YMK), peptides insert perpendicularly 
into the membrane and oligomerize to form transmembrane pores lined by the 
peptides themselves. The disruption in the integrity of the bacterial membrane
